stem: An engineer drops a Unity Catalog managed table by mistake and immediately asks whether the underlying files are already gone for good. The team needs an accurate answer about what happens to data files in cloud storage, because their recovery plan depends on whether any window exists at all.

option_texts.A: The data files are deleted after a recovery period expires, defaulting to seven days
option_texts.B: The data files are deleted the instant the command commits, leaving no window
option_texts.C: The data files are left in cloud storage permanently and must be removed by hand
option_texts.D: The data files are deleted only once VACUUM runs, with no recovery window at all

drill_answer_short: Managed table files are deleted after the recovery period expires, seven days by default
decision_hinge: When you drop a managed table, Databricks deletes the data files in cloud storage after the recovery period expires, which defaults to seven days.

plausible_options.B: asks whether the underlying files are already gone for good

C.signal: what happens to data files in cloud storage
C.requires_fact: Dropping a managed table causes Databricks to delete the data files in cloud storage, reducing storage costs.

eliminated_by.D: their recovery plan depends on whether any window exists at all

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — deletion really does follow the drop, but not instantly, which is the whole point for recovery
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — that is external table behaviour applied to a managed table
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — VACUUM removes unreferenced files from a live table rather than cleaning up a dropped one

stem: A table was registered over files that another team's pipeline writes and continues to own. After the table is dropped from the catalog, that other pipeline keeps reading the same files without interruption, and nobody restored anything to make that work.

option_texts.A: The table was managed, so dropping it removed metadata but kept the data files
option_texts.B: The table was external, so dropping it removed metadata but kept the data files
option_texts.C: The table was shallow cloned, so dropping it never touched the original files
option_texts.D: The table was protected by a retention threshold that blocked the file deletion

drill_answer_short: Dropping an external table removes the metadata but leaves the underlying files
decision_hinge: When you drop an external table, Unity Catalog removes the table metadata but does not delete the underlying data files.

plausible_options.C: that other pipeline keeps reading the same files without interruption

A.signal: After the table is dropped from the catalog
A.requires_fact: When you drop a managed table, Databricks deletes the data files in cloud storage after the recovery period expires.

eliminated_by.D: nobody restored anything to make that work

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — the right description of drop behaviour, attached to the wrong table type
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — a clone also leaves the source untouched, but nothing here suggests one existed
distractor_traps.D: T5: right diagnosis, wrong symptom — a retention window delays deletion rather than preserving files indefinitely

stem: A service principal needs read-only access to exactly one table in a governed catalog, and the security review insists on the smallest set of grants that makes the query work. Nothing beyond reading that single table should become possible. Select the TWO grants that must accompany SELECT on the table.

option_texts.A: USE CATALOG on the catalog that contains the table
option_texts.B: USE SCHEMA on the schema that contains the table
option_texts.C: MODIFY on the table so the reader can open a session
option_texts.D: SELECT on the schema so every table inside is readable
option_texts.E: ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog, narrowed later by review

drill_answer_short: Reading a table also needs USE CATALOG on its catalog and USE SCHEMA on its schema
decision_hinge: Unity Catalog privileges follow the object hierarchy, so a principal needs USE CATALOG on the parent catalog and USE SCHEMA on the parent schema in addition to SELECT on the table.

plausible_options.D: the security review insists on the smallest set of grants that makes the query work

eliminated_by.C: Nothing beyond reading that single table should become possible

E.signal: needs read-only access to exactly one table in a governed catalog
E.requires_fact: Privileges in Unity Catalog are granted on securable objects and inherited down the hierarchy from catalog to schema to table.

distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated requirement — MODIFY grants write access the review explicitly forbids
distractor_traps.D: T8: scope error — a schema-level SELECT opens every table in the schema, not just the one
distractor_traps.E: T4: breaks a stated requirement — the broadest possible grant is the opposite of least privilege

stem: An administrator granted a group SELECT on a specific table and the statement returned success. Members of that group still hit an insufficient permissions error the moment they query it, and no row filter or column mask has been defined anywhere on the table.

option_texts.A: The grant statement silently failed because the administrator did not own it
option_texts.B: The group is missing a second SELECT grant issued at the parent catalog level
option_texts.C: The group is missing traversal grants on the parent catalog and parent schema
option_texts.D: The grant needs a cluster restart before Unity Catalog begins enforcing it

drill_answer_short: SELECT alone is not enough — USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are needed to traverse to the table
decision_hinge: Unity Catalog privileges follow the object hierarchy, so a principal also needs USE CATALOG on the parent catalog and USE SCHEMA on the parent schema before a table-level SELECT can be exercised.

plausible_options.B: Members of that group still hit an insufficient permissions error

eliminated_by.D: no row filter or column mask has been defined anywhere on the table

distractor_traps.A: T4: breaks a stated requirement — the stem says the statement succeeded
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a catalog-level grant is involved, but it is USE CATALOG rather than another SELECT
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — no restart is required for a grant to take effect

stem: Before assigning a group a new, deliberately narrow set of permissions on a schema, a team has to be certain the group retains nothing it was granted previously. Nobody has an inventory of what was handed out over the years, and the team wants one statement that clears the slate without blocking future grants.

option_texts.A: Transfer ownership of the schema to the group so older grants stop applying
option_texts.B: DENY ALL PRIVILEGES on the schema to the group, overriding the prior grants
option_texts.C: SHOW GRANTS on the schema for the group, listing whatever was granted before
option_texts.D: REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES on the schema from the group, clearing prior grants

drill_answer_short: REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES removes existing grants and still allows new ones afterwards
decision_hinge: REVOKE removes previously granted privileges on a securable object from a principal, while leaving the principal eligible to receive new grants.

plausible_options.B: has to be certain the group retains nothing it was granted previously

A.signal: assigning a group a new, deliberately narrow set of permissions
A.requires_fact: Privileges on a Unity Catalog securable are granted and revoked from principals, and ownership is a separate concept from the granted privilege set.

eliminated_by.C: the team wants one statement that clears the slate

distractor_traps.A: T8: scope error — ownership confers broad control rather than clearing a privilege list
distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — an explicit denial also stops prior access, but it keeps blocking the narrow grants the team intends to add next
distractor_traps.C: T2: wrong layer — listing grants reports the state without changing it

stem: A masking function is already registered and the team now has to attach it to one sensitive column on a single existing table, so that unauthorised readers see a redacted value at query time. They want the statement that binds the function to that column specifically.

option_texts.A: ALTER TABLE accounts ALTER COLUMN card SET MASK mask_card
option_texts.B: ALTER TABLE accounts SET MASK mask_card ON COLUMN card
option_texts.C: ALTER TABLE accounts SET ROW FILTER mask_card ON (card)
option_texts.D: GRANT MASK mask_card ON COLUMN accounts.card TO analysts

drill_answer_short: A column mask is bound with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK
decision_hinge: Row filters and column masks are Unity Catalog access controls that restrict the rows and column values a user can see at query time, and a table-level control is bound to a single table using ALTER TABLE.

plausible_options.B: attach it to one sensitive column on a single existing table

C.signal: so that unauthorised readers see a redacted value at query time
C.requires_fact: Row filters restrict which rows a user can see in a table, whereas column masks restrict the column values a user can see.

eliminated_by.D: They want the statement that binds the function to that column specifically

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the right clause names in the wrong grammatical order for a column mask
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the row filter statement, which limits rows rather than redacting a value
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — masking is attached to the column, not granted as a privilege to a group

stem: A registered function decides which regions a caller may see, and the team must now bind it to one existing table so that unauthorised readers get fewer rows rather than redacted values. The function takes the region column as its argument and the binding has to name that argument.

option_texts.A: ALTER TABLE sales ALTER COLUMN region SET ROW FILTER region_filter
option_texts.B: ALTER TABLE sales SET ROW FILTER region_filter ON (region)
option_texts.C: ALTER TABLE sales ALTER COLUMN region SET MASK region_filter
option_texts.D: SET ROW FILTER region_filter ON TABLE sales TO COLUMN region

drill_answer_short: A row filter is bound with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER ... ON (column)
decision_hinge: Table-level row filters are bound to a single table using ALTER TABLE SET ROW FILTER and managed by the table owner.

plausible_options.A: The function takes the region column as its argument and the binding has to name that argument

C.signal: unauthorised readers get fewer rows rather than redacted values
C.requires_fact: Row filters restrict which rows a user can see in a table, while column masks restrict the column values returned.

eliminated_by.D: the team must now bind it to one existing table

distractor_traps.A: T3: confusable sibling — a filter applies to the table while naming a column argument, not to the column itself
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the column mask statement, which redacts values instead of removing rows
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — this statement shape does not exist

stem: A function must return the real diagnosis value to members of the doctors group and the literal CONFIDENTIAL to everyone else. A reviewer is checking the branch order, because an inverted condition would quietly expose the sensitive value to the wrong audience while still looking plausible in review.

option_texts.A: RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('diagnosis') THEN doctors ELSE 'CONFIDENTIAL' END
option_texts.B: RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('doctors') THEN 'CONFIDENTIAL' ELSE diagnosis END
option_texts.C: RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('doctors') THEN diagnosis ELSE 'CONFIDENTIAL' END
option_texts.D: RETURN CASE WHEN diagnosis IS NOT NULL THEN diagnosis ELSE 'CONFIDENTIAL' END

drill_answer_short: Group members get the real value; the ELSE branch returns the redacted literal
decision_hinge: A column mask is a function whose condition decides, at query time, which callers receive the real column value and which receive a redacted value instead.

plausible_options.D: A reviewer is checking the branch order

A.signal: the literal CONFIDENTIAL to everyone else
A.requires_fact: The group membership check takes the group name as its argument and the masking function returns the column value for permitted callers.

eliminated_by.B: must return the real diagnosis value to members of the doctors group

distractor_traps.A: T1: fabricated — the column name and the group name are swapped into each other's positions
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated requirement — this is the inverted branch the reviewer is looking for, redacting precisely the audience that should see the value
distractor_traps.D: T5: right diagnosis, wrong symptom — it branches on whether a value exists rather than on who is asking

stem: Hundreds of tables across one catalog carry columns holding the same category of sensitive data, and new tables appear every week. The team wants consistent masking applied everywhere without editing each table as it is created, and without maintaining a separate object per table.

option_texts.A: Grant the sensitive columns to nobody, so only table owners can read them at all
option_texts.B: Run ALTER TABLE to set a column mask on each table as part of its creation script
option_texts.C: Build a dynamic view over every table and point all consumers at the views instead
option_texts.D: Define an ABAC policy whose conditions match the governed tags on those columns

drill_answer_short: ABAC policies apply by governed tag, so new matching tables are covered automatically
decision_hinge: Databricks recommends ABAC policies when you need consistent row filtering and column masking across many tables, and when a securable object has the attributes targeted by a policy that policy takes effect automatically.

plausible_options.B: Hundreds of tables across one catalog carry columns holding the same category of sensitive data

A.requires_fact: A single ABAC policy can enforce consistent access rules across an entire metastore, catalog, or schema.

eliminated_by.C: without maintaining a separate object per table

distractor_traps.A: T4: breaks a stated requirement — blocking access entirely is not masking
distractor_traps.B: T8: scope error — per-table statements do work, but they must be repeated for every table forever
distractor_traps.C: T7: over-engineering — a view per table is the separate object the team is trying to avoid

stem: A governance lead is explaining how an ABAC policy knows which columns it should protect, given that the policy text never lists any table or column by name. An auditor wants to understand the mechanism that connects a single written policy to the specific data it ends up covering.

option_texts.A: Governed tags on the objects, which policy conditions match to select what is protected
option_texts.B: An explicit allowlist of table names, compiled into the policy when it is first created
option_texts.C: Column name pattern matching, which protects any column whose name looks sensitive
option_texts.D: The ownership chain, which protects whatever the policy author happens to own already

drill_answer_short: Governed tags are the attributes ABAC policy conditions match on
decision_hinge: Attributes represented through governed tags are used in policy conditions to identify which data a policy should protect.

plausible_options.C: the policy text never lists any table or column by name

eliminated_by.B: the policy text never lists any table or column by name

D.signal: the mechanism that connects a single written policy to the specific data it ends up covering
D.requires_fact: When a securable object has the attributes targeted by a policy, that policy takes effect automatically across the metastore, catalog, or schema.

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — matching on an attribute is right, but the attribute is an assigned tag rather than the column's name
distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated requirement — an allowlist is exactly the naming the stem says is absent
distractor_traps.D: T2: wrong layer — ownership governs who may administer an object, not which objects a policy covers
